opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the naming has had a real effect, and probably in the direction of making people underrate progress.

The basic dynamic is that GPT-4 came out in early 2023 and was a big, salient jump. Then for a long stretch afterwards, OpenAI kept shipping models that were meaningfully better but called them things like GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-4o, and then the o-series reasoning models. None of these got the "GPT-5" label for a long time. So if you're a casual observer anchoring on the version number, it looks like we went from GPT-3 to GPT-4, and then things kind of plateaued. "We've been stuck on GPT-4 for ages, maybe scaling is hitting a wall."

But if you look at actual capabilities, especially on harder agentic tasks, coding, math, and long multi-step work, the gains over that period were large. The reasoning models in particular were a pretty big qualitative shift on some benchmarks. Cumulatively, the improvement from the original GPT-4 to what was available a year or two later was arguably comparable to some of the earlier generational jumps people treated as huge. It just came in a bunch of smaller increments with incremental-sounding names rather than one big reveal.

There's a more general point here: people's sense of progress is driven a lot by discrete, salient events, and a smooth trend that's split into many small releases feels less dramatic than the same total progress delivered all at once. So when GPT-5 eventually did come out, a lot of people compared it to their memory of the GPT-3 to GPT-4 jump and felt underwhelmed, even though the right comparison is to the original GPT-4, and on that comparison the gap is big.

I'd add a caveat: I don't think naming is the main driver of what informed people believe. People who track benchmarks or use these systems heavily mostly weren't fooled. But for the broader public, policymakers, and even some people in tech who aren't following closely, I think it plausibly contributed to a "progress is slowing" narrative that I think is mostly wrong, or at least much less supported than people assume. The more useful thing is to look at trend lines on things like the length of tasks AI systems can complete autonomously, rather than vibes from version numbers.

r001.rationale: The response says people anchor on GPT-4 branding, but does not mention Grok 3 or describe that comparison.

r002.rationale: It states that improved releases kept GPT-4-branded names and that this plausibly led people to underestimate progress.

r003.rationale: It gives no estimate of a little over an order of magnitude for progress from original GPT-4 to the best GPT-4o.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think the naming has mattered more than people might expect. The thing about GPT-4 is that it set this anchor in people's heads: there's GPT-3, then GPT-4, and so naturally everyone was waiting for GPT-5 as the next big step. And for a long time, GPT-5 just didn't come. Instead you got GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-4o, o1, o3, 4.5, and so on. So if you were following along from the outside and mostly tracking the headline version number, it looked like progress had stalled. Like, "it's been two years and we're still on 4."

But if you actually look at the capabilities, the models released under those confusing names were substantially better than the original GPT-4. The gap between GPT-4 at launch and something like o3 on reasoning, math, agentic coding tasks, is enormous, arguably bigger than some earlier version jumps. So I think the naming created a kind of illusion of a plateau. People conflated "no new integer" with "no new capability."

There's also a second effect, which is that when OpenAI held back the GPT-5 name, it raised expectations for what GPT-5 would have to be. The name became a promise. And when a model with that name finally ships, it gets judged against the accumulated hype rather than against the previous model, which can make a perfectly solid incremental release feel disappointing. So you get this weird dynamic where the naming both understates progress during the gap and then sets up a letdown when the number finally increments.

I think the deeper lesson is that version numbers are just a bad proxy. The thing I'd want people to track is something like: how long and how complex are the tasks these systems can do autonomously, and how fast is that growing? That's a much more informative signal than whether the label says 4 or 5, and on that metric, progress has been pretty steady and pretty fast, regardless of what the branding was doing.

r001.rationale: The response says people mistook the lack of a new integer label for stalled progress, but it does not mention Grok 3 or identify recent GPT-4-branded releases as the comparison baseline.

r002.rationale: It states that keeping improved releases under GPT-4-era names made outside observers think progress had stalled, creating an illusion of a plateau.

r003.rationale: The response describes improvements as substantial but gives no estimate of a little over an order of magnitude and does not make that claim about the best GPT-4o.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s made progress look slower than it actually is. If you keep calling successive models some version of GPT-4, people naturally think, “Well, we’re still on GPT-4. How much has really changed?” But the name isn’t a consistent unit of capability. You can have substantial improvements in how useful a model is, or how cheaply and quickly you can run it, without changing that headline number.

And then the reverse can happen when you finally call something GPT-5: people might perceive a big discontinuity even if the underlying progress was relatively continuous. So I’d put much more weight on what the systems can actually do than on whether the company has decided to increment the number.

r001.rationale: The response discusses successive GPT-4 names generally, but does not identify recent GPT-4 releases as the comparison baseline for Grok 3 versus the original GPT-4.

r002.rationale: It says that keeping improved models under GPT-4 branding makes people think little has changed and makes progress look slower than it is.

r003.rationale: The response gives no estimate of progress from original GPT-4 to GPT-4o, let alone a little over an order of magnitude.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s probably made progress look slower than it actually is. If you release a model called GPT-4, and then substantially improve it but keep calling it some variant of GPT-4, people can get the impression that we’re still basically at the same point. Whereas if you’d called one of those improvements GPT-5, I think people would have perceived a much bigger jump.

Of course, the name itself isn’t evidence about how much progress there’s been. You should look at what the models can actually do. But in practice, people use these version numbers as a rough guide, and there’s no standardized relationship between a new number and a particular amount of capability improvement.

r002.rationale: It says keeping the GPT-4 name for substantially improved models can make people think progress is slower and that the models remain at the same point.
